lessons.title: The Origin of the Universe and Stewardship

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All six world religions affirm that the universe has a divine origin, though their accounts differ significantly — from Genesis 1 (Christianity/Judaism) to Ik Onkar (Sikhism) to paticca-samuppada without a creator (Buddhism). Humanists accept the Big Bang and evolution as the scientific account of origins.
  • Christian stewardship draws on Genesis 1:28 and Psalm 8:6, developed in Laudato Si’ (2015). Jewish tikkun olam and bal tashchit, Islamic khalifah, Hindu ahimsa, Sikh sewa and Buddhist paticca-samuppada all ground environmental responsibility in their own theological frameworks.
  • The debate between dominion and stewardship within Christianity, and between religious and non-religious approaches to environmental ethics, is a key evaluative axis for this theme.
before.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers a large topic — for ‘Explain two beliefs’ questions, focus on giving two distinct religious traditions with one source of authority each. Don’t just describe what each religion says; explain why it matters — for example, why the concept of khalifah leads Muslims to environmental responsibility, or why tikkun olam gives Jews a particular motivation for environmental action. For 15-mark evaluations, always include a non-religious perspective (Humanist Climate Action, Hawking, Dawkins) alongside at least two religious views, and reach a justified conclusion.

lessons.title: The Sanctity of Life, Abortion and Euthanasia

before.content_html:
The Value of Human Life: A Universal Question

When does human life begin? When, if ever, is it acceptable to end it? In the UK, abortion has been legal (under certain conditions) since 1967, and the debate about assisted dying continues in Parliament. Most major religions take a position on both questions, ranging from absolute prohibition to qualified permission.

The central tension runs between two principles. The sanctity of life argument holds that human life has an intrinsic, inviolable worth that cannot be forfeited by circumstance. Against this stands the quality of life argument: that what matters is not merely biological existence but whether life is experienced as meaningful and free from excessive suffering.

Key Fact

The sanctity of life holds that every human life has intrinsic, God-given worth from conception to natural death. The quality of life view holds that what matters is whether life contains sufficient wellbeing and freedom from suffering to be worth living. These two principles underpin every religious and non-religious argument on abortion and euthanasia.

Legal and Human Rights Context

On euthanasia, the Dignity in Dying campaign argues that individuals should have the right to end their own suffering. The ‘Right to Choose’ framing in the abortion debate likewise centres on personal autonomy over a religious conception of sanctity. Both campaigns reflect a wider shift in how the state and public discourse frame bodily autonomy.

The Abortion Act 1967 made abortion legal in Great Britain (not Northern Ireland, where different legislation applied until 2019) up to 24 weeks of pregnancy, provided two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy would involve a greater risk to the woman’s physical or mental health, or to any existing children, than terminating it. After 24 weeks, abortion is permitted only in exceptional circumstances — for example, where continuing the pregnancy would endanger the woman’s life or where there is a serious foetal abnormality. The 24-week threshold roughly corresponds with the point of foetal viability outside the womb, though this point has shifted as neonatal medicine has advanced. The law does not frame abortion as a right but as a permitted medical procedure under defined conditions — a distinction that both pro-choice and pro-life campaigners continue to contest.

Christianity and Catholicism

Christianity teaches that human beings are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27 — imago Dei). Genesis 1:31 records God declaring all he had made ‘very good’, and Jeremiah 1:5 describes God knowing the prophet before his formation in the womb — both verses are read as affirming the value of life from its earliest stages.

The Catholic Church takes the most explicit position. The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 2270, states that human life must be respected and protected from the moment of conception. On euthanasia, Evangelium Vitae (Pope John Paul II, 1995), paragraph 65, teaches that the direct and voluntary killing of an innocent person is gravely wrong, even to relieve suffering. The Church supports palliative care and the Sacrament of the Sick for the dying. Some other Christian denominations have expressed qualified openness to assisted dying in limited circumstances.

Key Fact

Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 2270 states: “Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.” This makes abortion morally impermissible for Catholics regardless of circumstances. Evangelium Vitae (1995), paragraph 65, extends the same absolute prohibition to euthanasia, describing it as a “grave violation of the law of God.”

Judaism

Jewish law (halakha) centres on pikuach nefesh — preserving life overrides almost all other commandments, including Shabbat (Talmud Bavli Yoma 84b). The Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches that whoever destroys a single soul destroys an entire world; whoever saves one saves an entire world.

On abortion, the Mishnah Oholot 7:6 rules that where the mother’s life is endangered the foetus’s life may be sacrificed to save hers — the foetus is not a full legal person. Most Orthodox authorities permit abortion only to save the mother; many Conservative and Reform rabbis permit it more broadly. Judaism does not share the Catholic absolute prohibition. On euthanasia, the tradition overwhelmingly forbids actively hastening death, though there is more flexibility on withdrawing treatment that merely prolongs dying.

Judaism is not a monolithic tradition, and different movements apply halakha with differing degrees of strictness. Orthodox Judaism generally holds that abortion is prohibited except where the mother’s life is in genuine danger — the foetus has sanctity but does not yet hold the full legal status of a person (nefesh). Conservative Judaism tends to permit abortion in a somewhat wider range of cases, including serious foetal abnormalities or severe risk to the mother’s mental health. Reform Judaism places considerable weight on the woman’s autonomy and wellbeing, and generally supports her right to make the decision in consultation with her rabbi and healthcare providers. Across all branches, the view that the foetus is a potential life deserving serious moral consideration — not a mere clump of cells — is shared; the disagreement is about how much that potential life’s weight can be overridden by other considerations. In exam answers, this internal diversity is a strength: it shows you understand that “Judaism teaches X” is always a simplification.

Islam

Islam teaches that human life is a trust (amanah) from Allah and that only Allah has the right to give or take life. The Qur’an (5:32) teaches that to save one life is as if to save all of humanity; Qur’an 6:151 commands: do not kill your children.

Most Islamic scholars regard abortion as forbidden (haram) after ensoulment — when Allah breathes a soul into the foetus (Qur’an 32:9). Different schools debate when ensoulment occurs, but abortion after this point is regarded as very grave; some scholars permit it in very limited circumstances before that point. Most Islamic authorities forbid euthanasia, seeing it as usurping Allah’s sovereignty over life and death.

Hinduism

Hindu teaching sees all life as sacred because it contains atman — the universal soul. The Bhagavad Gita (2:17) teaches that the eternal soul is indestructible, passing through many lives (samsāra); killing interrupts a soul’s journey, not merely a biological life.

The principle of ahimsa (non-violence, Yajur Veda 40–43) leads most Hindu authorities to oppose abortion and euthanasia, as both involve deliberate harm to a being containing atman. There is no single central authority issuing binding rulings, and in practice attitudes vary widely; the question of whether withdrawing futile treatment differs morally from active killing is debated.

Sikhism

Sikhs believe human life is a precious gift from God — an opportunity to draw closer to the divine and escape samsāra. The soul in all living beings is universal (Guru Granth Sahib 441), and Sikh Gurus explicitly condemned female infanticide. Sikh teaching generally discourages abortion, regarding it as interference with God-given natural processes, though many Sikhs weigh individual circumstances. On euthanasia, the consensus is that hastening death is wrong, though withdrawing futile treatment that merely prolongs dying is more permissible.

Buddhism

Buddhism’s first of the Five Precepts is to refrain from taking life. Both abortion and euthanasia involve the intentional ending of life, violating the Precept and creating negative kamma. Buddhist teaching is not absolutist, however: the Dalai Lama has suggested that karuṇā (compassion) — working with dukkha rather than simply prolonging it — may make euthanasia an act of compassion in some circumstances. Theravāda teaching is generally against abortion, since conception marks the start of a new life in the rebirth cycle, but there is no central institution issuing binding rulings and positions vary.

Non-Religious Views

Peter Singer’s concept of speciesism challenges the automatic special status of human life: what matters morally, he argues, is an organism’s capacity for conscious experience, not its species. A foetus at an early stage may therefore have less moral status than a developed non-human animal. Dignity in Dying and similar campaigns use a situationist approach: rather than applying an absolute rule, they ask what is best for this particular person in these circumstances.

Humanists argue that the emphasis should be on ‘life before death’ — improving the quality of the life that is lived. On abortion, many Humanists support a woman’s right to choose. On euthanasia, they support the right of individuals facing terminal suffering to choose the timing and manner of their death, seeing this as an expression of human dignity and self-determination.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 15-mark evaluation question on sanctity of life topics, the most common failure is giving only one side. You need at least one argument for the statement, at least one against, and a clear personal conclusion. Use precise sources: Catechism 2270 (Catholic on abortion), pikuach nefesh / Talmud Yoma 84b (Jewish priority of life), Qur’an 5:32 (Islamic sanctity), and Peter Singer’s speciesism (non-religious challenge). Remember: Dignity in Dying and ‘Right to Choose’ are the named non-religious organisations on this topic. Spelling, punctuation and grammar count for 5% of the 15-mark question — write in continuous prose, not bullet points.

lessons.title: Beliefs about Death and the Afterlife

before.content_html:
What Happens After Death?

Every religious tradition has developed teachings about what happens after physical death. These beliefs shape how adherents understand the purpose of earthly life, how they treat the dying, how they mourn and how they think about justice in a world where wrongdoing often appears to go unpunished. Humanists, by contrast, hold that death is the end of personal existence. This lesson examines beliefs about death and the afterlife across six religious traditions and a non-religious worldview, following the canonical order: Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Non-religious.

Christianity

Christians believe in life after death grounded in the resurrection of Jesus. The New Testament affirms that Jesus rose from the dead and that this promises resurrection for all believers. Jesus tells Martha in John 11:24–27: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die.” Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:42–44) describes the resurrection body as imperishable, glorious and spiritual, in contrast to the physical body that is perishable and weak.

Christian beliefs about the afterlife include heaven (eternal life with God), hell (separation from God) and, in Catholic theology, purgatory (a state of purification after death for souls not yet ready for heaven). The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1020–1023) describes the particular judgement each person faces at death and the final vision of God in heaven. Catechism 1030 addresses purgatory and 1033 affirms the possibility of damnation for those who permanently reject God’s love. Protestant denominations generally reject purgatory, holding that the believer passes directly from death to the presence of God.

Key Fact

Christian afterlife beliefs: heaven (eternal life with God), hell (eternal separation from God), purgatory (Catholic: state of purification). Scripture: John 11:24–27 (resurrection promise); 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 (nature of the resurrection body). Catholic teaching: CCC 1020–1023 (judgement and heaven); CCC 1030 (purgatory); CCC 1033 (damnation).

Judaism

Jewish beliefs about the afterlife are more diverse than Christian ones, and in many strands of Judaism this life takes priority over speculation about the next. The Hebrew Bible contains the concept of sheol — a shadowy, undifferentiated realm of the dead rather than a place of reward or punishment. Later Jewish thought, especially in the period of the Second Temple, developed concepts of resurrection, judgement and olam ha-ba (the world to come).

Orthodox Jews affirm bodily resurrection and divine judgement; Reform Jews tend to understand olam ha-ba more metaphorically or focus on legacy and the memory of the righteous. Jewish funerary practice (see the lesson on funeral rites) reflects these beliefs — burial rather than cremation is traditional, expressing the hope of resurrection.

Islam

The Islamic concept of the afterlife is called akhirah. Islam teaches that after death, the soul enters a state of waiting (Barzakh) until the Day of Judgement. On that day, all people will be raised and judged by Allah according to their deeds and faith. The Qur’an teaches that Allah has the power to resurrect the dead: Qur’an 46:33 affirms that the One who created the heavens and the earth is not unable to resurrect the dead. Qur’an 3:16 speaks of those who pray for forgiveness and protection from the punishment of the fire — affirming both the reality of hell (Jahannam) and the hope of paradise (Jannah).

Islamic funeral practice is closely connected to the belief in akhirah: the body is washed and shrouded, buried promptly and placed facing Makkah. The speed and simplicity of Islamic burial reflect the belief that the body should be returned to the earth from which it was created, ready for resurrection.

Hinduism

Hindu beliefs about death centre on the cycle of samsara (the cycle of birth, death and rebirth). The Bhagavad Gita (2:12–13) teaches that the atman (the eternal self or soul) is never truly destroyed: just as a person changes clothes, the soul moves from one body to another at death. The ultimate goal is moksha — liberation from the cycle of rebirth and union with Brahman (the ultimate reality). The path to moksha may take many lifetimes. Karma (the moral law of cause and effect) determines the conditions of each reincarnation.

Sikhism

Sikh beliefs about death are closely related to Hindu ideas but with a distinctive theological emphasis. Like Hindus, Sikhs believe in samsara (the cycle of rebirth) and karma. The soul’s goal is mukti — liberation from the cycle of rebirth and union with Waheguru (God). The Guru Granth Sahib (page 13) affirms that the soul that truly meditates on God’s name achieves liberation. In Sikhism, mukti comes not through ritual or caste but through God’s grace (nadar), devotion (bhakti) and righteous living. Death is not feared but understood as the soul’s return to its source.

Key Fact

Sikh afterlife belief: samsara (cycle of rebirth driven by karma), with mukti (liberation and union with Waheguru) as the goal. Guru Granth Sahib 13 affirms that meditating on God’s name leads to liberation. Mukti is achieved through God’s grace, devotion and righteous living — not through caste or ritual.

Buddhism

Buddhist afterlife teaching is distinctive because of the teaching of anatta (no fixed self). If there is no permanent self, what is it that is “reborn”? Buddhists explain this through the analogy of a flame passed from candle to candle: something is transmitted, but it is not the same flame, nor a completely different one. What carries forward is kamma (the Pali term for the moral force of intentional actions) and the mental formations (sankhāras) that arise from it — not an unchanging soul.

The goal of Buddhist practice is nibbāna — the complete cessation of the cycle of rebirth, achieved when kamma is exhausted and craving is extinguished. The Triratna tradition includes members who interpret rebirth not as literal life-to-life reincarnation but as moment-to-moment arising and passing away of experience — a more psychological reading of the doctrine.

All three traditions — Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism — teach some form of samsara (the cycle of rebirth). However, they differ in what is reborn. Hinduism affirms the atman (eternal, unchanging soul) as what transmigrates. Sikhism also affirms the soul’s journey across lives toward God. Buddhism denies a permanent soul (anatta) — what transmigrates is a stream of kamma and consciousness, not an unchanging entity. The goals also differ: Hinduism seeks moksha (union with Brahman), Sikhism seeks mukti (union with Waheguru), Buddhism seeks nibbāna (cessation of rebirth through extinguishing of craving).

Non-Religious and Humanist Views

Humanists understand death as the end of personal existence. There is no afterlife, no soul that survives the body, no resurrection or reincarnation. The Humanist tradition emphasises making the most of the one life we have and finding meaning in relationships, achievements, contribution to society and the legacy we leave behind. Grief is real and important; Humanist funeral ceremonies mark the significance of the life that has ended without religious language. The emphasis is on “life before death” rather than consolation from promises of an afterlife.

Believers often argue that afterlife teaching provides motivation for ethical living: if actions have consequences beyond this life (judgement, karma, kamma), people have reason to live well even when no human authority can see them. Critics argue the opposite: that focus on the next life can devalue this life and that the Humanist emphasis on “life before death” provides a stronger motivation to improve the world now. This is a productive axis for evaluation in extended-response questions.

flashcard_questions.q: Which New Testament passage affirms the resurrection body as imperishable and spiritual?

flashcard_questions.a: Purgatory — the state of purification after death for souls destined for heaven.
flashcard_questions.q: What does the Catholic Catechism (CCC 1030) address?

flashcard_questions.a: A shadowy underworld in the Hebrew Bible — an early concept of where the dead go, before later ideas of resurrection.
flashcard_questions.q: What is sheol in Jewish belief?

flashcard_questions.a: Hebrew for 'the world to come' — the Jewish afterlife, where the righteous enjoy closeness to God.
The Islamic belief in the afterlife, including Barzakh, Day of Judgement, Jannah and Jahannam.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Qur'an verse affirms Allah's power to resurrect the dead?

flashcard_questions.a: The soul (atman) is never destroyed — like changing clothes, it moves from body to body at death.
flashcard_questions.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita 2:12–13 teach about the atman?

flashcard_questions.a: Liberation from the cycle of samsara and union with Brahman — the ultimate goal of Hindu spiritual life.
Liberation from samsara and union with Waheguru (God), achieved through God's grace and devotion.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Guru Granth Sahib page affirms that meditating on God's name leads to liberation?

flashcard_questions.a: Buddhism denies a fixed soul (anatta) — kamma transmits, not an unchanging self.
flashcard_questions.q: Why is Buddhist rebirth distinctive compared to Hindu and Sikh rebirth?

flashcard_questions.a: Death is the end of personal existence — no afterlife, soul or resurrection; emphasis is on 'life before death'.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the Humanist view on life after death?

practice_questions.text: Give two Christian beliefs about the afterlife.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: heaven (eternal life with God) / hell (separation from God) / purgatory (Catholic: state of purification) / resurrection of the body / judgement. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What does 'akhirah' mean in Islamic belief?
practice_questions.marks: The Islamic belief in the afterlife — encompassing the period from death through the Day of Judgement to the eternal states of Jannah (paradise) and Jahannam (hell). [2 marks — 1 for identification, 1 for explanation]

practice_questions.text: Describe Sikh beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Samsara (cycle of rebirth), kamma, mukti (liberation and union with Waheguru), Guru Granth Sahib 13, God's grace (nadar), death as the soul's return to its source.
Secure: Two clear points (samsara, mukti) with some development.
Developing: One or two features briefly described.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the teaching about samsara influences the beliefs of Hindus and Buddhists differently.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed comparisons — Hinduism affirms an eternal atman that transmigrates toward moksha; Buddhism denies a fixed self (anatta), with kamma transmitting not a soul but moral force toward nibbana. Both agree samsara is the problem; they differ on what is reborn and the goal.
Secure: Two points with some comparison and development.
Developing: One comparison developed.
Emerging: Simple statement about one tradition.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting beliefs about life after death.
Refer to sources of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly contrasting beliefs from different traditions (e.g. Christian resurrection — John 11:24-27, 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 — versus Humanist 'death is the end'; or Islamic akhirah — Qur'an 46:33 — versus Buddhist nibbana without a fixed self) each developed with source and explanation of significance.
Secure: Two contrasting views, one source, some development.
Developing: Two views briefly stated.
Emerging: One view only.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in an afterlife is essential to living a good life.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Islamic teaching of akhirah (Day of Judgement) provides direct motivation for ethical living — actions have eternal consequences (Qur'an 46:33).
• Hindu karma and samsara mean that how one lives this life determines the conditions of future lives — belief in rebirth incentivises moral behaviour.
• Christian belief in heaven and hell (CCC 1033) provides a framework of ultimate justice: wrongdoers cannot escape divine judgement.
• Sikh mukti — achievable through devotion and righteous living — gives the ethical life a cosmic significance beyond mere social approval.
Arguments against:
• Humanists live ethically without any afterlife belief — moral behaviour is grounded in empathy, reason and care for others in this life alone.
• Buddhist Triratna tradition shows that afterlife beliefs can be interpreted psychologically (moment-to-moment rebirth) without undermining the ethical commitments of the Five Precepts.
• Jesus's teaching in the Gospels includes living ethically for the sake of the Kingdom of God, not merely to avoid hell.
• Secular psychological research shows that ethical behaviour is shaped primarily by environment, relationships and social norms — not by theological beliefs about the afterlife.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides sustained, multiple traditions referenced, Humanist view included, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

lessons.title: Funeral Rites and Evaluating Life and Death

practice_questions.text: Give two features of an Islamic funeral.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: prompt burial (within 24 hours) / ritual washing of the body / wrapping in white shroud (kafan) / Janaza prayer / body placed facing Makkah / no coffin (where possible). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is 'shiva' in Jewish mourning practice?
practice_questions.marks: The seven-day period of intense mourning observed after a Jewish funeral, during which the bereaved stay at home, receive visitors and are supported by the community. [2 marks — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Hindu funeral rites reflect Hindu beliefs about death.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cremation linked explicitly to belief in samsara (soul released from body), the atman's continuing journey, the role of the eldest son, mantras and Bhagavad Gita recitation, scattering of ashes in a sacred river — each linked to why it reflects Hindu belief.
Secure: Two clear features with some explanation of belief-link.
Developing: One or two features described, belief connection weak.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Humanist funerals reflect Humanist beliefs about death.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Humanist celebrant creates personalised ceremony; no reference to God or afterlife (because Humanists believe death is the end of personal existence); focus on the life lived, memory and legacy; grief acknowledged honestly; reflects 'life before death' emphasis.
Secure: Two points linking Humanist practice to Humanist belief.
Developing: One point developed.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting religious views on the correct way to treat a dead body.
Refer to sources of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two contrasting practices (e.g. Islamic burial — kafan, qiblah, speed — rooted in belief in resurrection of the body and akhirah (Qur'an 46:33); Buddhist cremation — reflecting anicca, the example of the Buddha, transfer of merit to the deceased) each developed with a source of authority and explanation of why the practice flows from the belief.
Secure: Two contrasting views, one source, some development.
Developing: Two practices described without full belief-link.
Emerging: One practice only.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious funeral rites are more meaningful than Humanist funerals.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Catholic funerals connect the bereaved to centuries of tradition, scripture (John 11:25) and the community of the Church (CCC 1684-1690) — this communal dimension adds significance beyond the individual.
• Religious funerals affirm resurrection or rebirth, giving mourners hope that death is not the final word.
• Islamic, Jewish and Sikh funeral rites are precise and purposeful — each element (kafan, shiva, Kirtan Sohila) carries theological weight that a purely secular ceremony may lack.
Arguments against:
• Humanist funerals are personally tailored to the individual's life, values and character — supporters argue this is more genuinely meaningful than following a set liturgy.
• For the non-religious bereaved, a religious funeral may feel alien or dishonest — a Humanist ceremony may better reflect the reality of the person's life and beliefs.
• The purpose of a funeral is to comfort the bereaved and honour the dead — Humanist ceremonies achieve this without requiring shared theological commitments.
• Research on funeral satisfaction consistently finds that personalisation is the factor most linked to mourners feeling the ceremony was meaningful.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides sustained, multiple religious traditions referenced, Humanist view included, clear justified conclusion that weighs the evidence.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.
